conditions.name: Ligament sprain

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

Weight-bear as pain allows
Review at 5-7 days if not settling

triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

Physiotherapy

exam.step: Wash the wound immediately with soap and running water for 15 minutes -- do this before anything else, including before seeking further care
exam.positive: The single most effective life-saving intervention, and it is entirely within the patient's own immediate control

exam.step: Categorise the exposure per WHO criteria (touching/feeding an animal = category I, no PEP; minor scratches without bleeding = category II; bites, broken skin, or mucous membrane contact = category III, needs RIG plus vaccine)
exam.positive: Determines exactly what treatment is needed -- not every animal contact needs the full regimen, but every category III exposure needs it started immediately

exam.step: Ask about the animal: was it a known, healthy, vaccinated pet available for observation, or a stray/wild animal that cannot be observed?
exam.positive: A healthy pet dog available for 10 days' observation changes the risk calculation, but PEP should still be started immediately and only stopped if the animal remains healthy throughout observation

labs.test: Clinical risk categorisation (WHO exposure category)
labs.confirms: The basis for the PEP decision -- there is no diagnostic test that can safely rule out rabies exposure before symptoms develop

labs.test: Direct fluorescent antibody testing of the animal (if it dies/is euthanised)
labs.confirms: Can confirm or exclude rabies in the animal, but PEP should never be delayed waiting for this result

conditions.name: Rabies (animal bite exposure)

triage.label: Emergency
triage.action: Call emergency services or go to an emergency department now

conditions.summary: Any bite, scratch, or lick on broken skin/mucous membrane from a dog, cat, monkey or other mammal in a rabies-endemic area (including almost all of India) needs to be treated as a possible rabies exposure -- not diagnosed by waiting for symptoms. Once symptoms of rabies itself develop (agitation, hydrophobia, paralysis), the disease is essentially 100% fatal -- there is no treatment at that stage. This is why the response to a bite is about IMMEDIATE wound care and post-exposure prophylaxis, not observation. India accounts for the largest share of the world's human rabies deaths, almost entirely from dog bites, and almost entirely because prophylaxis was delayed, incomplete, or not started at all -- not because prophylaxis failed. No dedicated 'animal bite' evidence node exists in this checker; the wound itself is captured only as a generic open wound, assessed on history.
workup: Immediately wash the wound with soap and running water for a full 15 minutes -- the single most effective, cheapest life-saving step, and it works even hours later if not yet done
Start the WHO post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) vaccination schedule promptly -- do not wait for the animal to be observed or tested before starting
Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) into and around the wound for category III exposures (broken skin, mucous membrane contact, or bites) per WHO categorisation
Complete the FULL vaccination course as scheduled -- partial/incomplete courses are a major, genuinely documented cause of preventable deaths
Tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics for the wound itself, as for any bite wound

exam.step: Look for fang puncture marks, local swelling, bruising, and pain out of proportion to the visible injury
exam.positive: The genuine local signs of a significant bite -- their presence or absence helps gauge severity but does not exclude systemic envenomation

exam.step: Ask about bleeding from the bite site, gums, or elsewhere, and assess for neurological symptoms (drooping eyelids, blurred vision, difficulty swallowing or breathing)
exam.positive: Signs of systemic envenomation needing urgent antivenom -- a genuine emergency

exam.step: Try to identify or safely photograph the snake, without attempting to catch or kill it
exam.positive: Can help guide antivenom choice, though treatment should never be delayed to obtain this

labs.test: 20-minute whole blood clotting test, or formal coagulation studies
labs.confirms: A genuine, practical bedside test for coagulopathy from viper envenomation

labs.test: Renal function and urine output monitoring
labs.confirms: Screens for acute kidney injury, a genuine complication of significant envenomation

conditions.name: Snake bite envenomation
aka: Sarpa Visha (classical correlate, NOT applicable clinically -- see below)

triage.label: Emergency
triage.action: Call emergency services or go to an emergency department now

conditions.summary: A bite from a venomous snake, causing local swelling/pain and, with significant envenomation, systemic effects (bleeding tendency, neurological weakness, or kidney injury depending on species). A genuine medical emergency -- antivenom is the only effective treatment for significant envenomation, and rapid transfer to hospital is essential. DELIBERATELY NO Ayurveda content included, matching this bundle's existing Rabies precedent: any delay seeking a home or alternative remedy for a possible envenomation is genuinely dangerous.
workup: Immediate emergency transfer to a hospital with antivenom available -- do NOT attempt to suck out venom, apply a tourniquet, or cut the wound, all of which are genuinely harmful and outdated
Immobilise the bitten limb and keep the patient as still as possible to slow venom spread, while arranging transport
Antivenom administration in hospital, guided by clinical severity and, where available, the snake's identification
Monitor for bleeding, neurological symptoms (drooping eyelids, difficulty swallowing/breathing), and kidney function

redFlags.label: Possible sepsis
redFlags.message: A fever together with confusion, very fast breathing, mottled skin or a collapsing blood pressure can mean infection is affecting the whole body.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

redFlags.label: Rash that does not fade under pressure
redFlags.message: Spots that stay visible when a glass is pressed on them, alongside feeling unwell, can be a sign of bacteria in the bloodstream.

redFlags.label: Possible severe allergic reaction
redFlags.message: Swelling of the throat or tongue with difficulty breathing after a food, sting, or medicine can close the airway within minutes.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Reduced consciousness
redFlags.message: Being difficult to rouse, or drifting in and out of awareness, always needs immediate assessment whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Place the person on their side if unresponsive.

redFlags.label: Possible stroke
redFlags.message: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment works only within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now and note the exact time symptoms began.

redFlags.label: Seizure
redFlags.message: A first seizure needs assessment to find the cause and to advise on driving and safety.
redFlags.action: Seek urgent assessment today. Call emergency services if the seizure lasted over five minutes or a second one followed.

redFlags.label: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding
redFlags.message: Vomiting blood, or passing black tarry stools, means bleeding inside the digestive tract.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: New jaundice
redFlags.message: Yellowing of the skin or eyes always needs blood tests to find out why.

redFlags.label: Sudden loss of vision
redFlags.message: Sight lost suddenly in one or both eyes needs assessment the same hour, whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Thoughts of self-harm
redFlags.message: Thoughts of harming yourself or of being better off dead deserve help today. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out.
redFlags.action: Contact your doctor, a crisis line, or go to an emergency department now. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services.

redFlags.label: New confusion coming on over hours or days
redFlags.message: Confusion that has come on over hours or days, or that comes and goes through the day, is delirium until proven otherwise. It is caused by something else -- an infection, a drug, pain, retention -- and that cause needs finding today.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Take a list of all medications. Call emergency services if they are drowsy, feverish or cannot be roused properly.

redFlags.label: Limb-threatening injury
redFlags.message: An open wound down to the bone, a limb that has gone cold or pale, or pain that keeps building far beyond what the injury explains, can mean the blood supply or the muscle compartment is compromised. Tissue can be lost within hours.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now. Do not eat or drink in case surgery is needed. Keep the limb still and at heart level.

disclaimer: This tool provides information about possible causes of symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it cannot examine you. It does not replace assessment by a qualified clinician. If you feel very unwell, or your symptoms are getting rapidly worse, seek medical help immediately regardless of what this tool says.
